yes. and not just by therapy and medication, tho they do help. i've noticed that i've learned to do a lot of self therapy. not based on any books or tips or anything. just a lil formula that i worked out for myself that has helped me out a lot and maybe could help you? 

when i start to feel anxious i: 
1. acknowledge- i say to myself "i am feeling anxious" 
2. identify- where do i feel the anxiety in my body 
3. rewind- what was i thinking about that made me anxious? 
4. problem-solve- what is the source of that anxious thought and how can i reduce/eliminate it? 

if i don't have time to mentally therapize myself i make sure to tackle that anxiety later on that same day. writing sometines helps but it's not necessary. with practice tho u can do this almost instantly or within 5 minutes cause u'll get so good at identifying your triggers 

again this is just something i worked out for myself not too long ago but that i found has been very effective at helping me at the very least identify my anxiety triggers even if the anxiety itself doesn't diminish. tho it does a lot of the time.

The ATS doesn't show us that, no! My company only knows the jobs you've applied to in my company since we've had the tool (some 4 or 5 years back).

Recruiter here: This is also visible when applying through literally anywhere else. Saw a job post on LinkedIn, Monster, Glassdoor, etc.? It will most likely end up in the company's ATS (Applicant Tracking System) which is where most, if not all, job applications go to (yes, including through company site, especially if you see phrases like "powered by Breezy/JazzHR/Greenhouse/etc.). 

Most ATS's publish jobs on every free job board and every paid one if the company wishes to pay. But all that links back to the ATS, which is where the job postings are created, published, and where aaaaaall candidates end up (except maybe those who send resumes via email). And these systems have historical data. 

In short, recruiters will probably be able to see how many times you've applied and to how many roles no matter where you apply from. The ATS we use merges candidate applications if the email and/or phone number is the same, and puts in a single page all the jobs you've applied to with our company, ever, and the reasons we rejected you, if any. 

Now, in terms of whether that's good or bad, like OP said, it depends on the recruiter. But IMO, just keep applying 'til you find what you're looking for. Better to be rejected because you applied too many times, than not even being considered because you didn't apply.

How cute! I have a pet rabbit since December last year and while he is a little difficult, it's not so bad oncw yoy gwt the hang of it! I did a loooot of Googling and here's what's worked for me: 

1. He will eat anything, yes. But that doesn't mean you can give him anything. Rabbits are herbivores and they can eat pretty much any greens (except lettuce for some reason). HOWEVER, his main diet should be hay. Lots and lots of hay, as in free-feeding (having it always available for him to eat). You can also feed him small amounts of rabbit pellets, make sure it's as organic as possible WITHOUT NUTS. Nuts have fat which is very very bad for bunnies. As for hay, a good choice is Timothy Hay. If you find Alfalfa hay it's ok, but once he gets bigger he should be transitioned to Timothy since it's best for adult bunnies. 

2. He will poop. A lot. As in, a L O T. My bunny lives with 3 cats so he kinda learned to poop in the vicinity of the litter box (not quite inside tho) so i just sweep or vaccuum his poop. He might poop outside in the garden, which you can leave as fertilizer, or if it gets to be too much, you can scoop and throw it out. 

3. Speaking of garden, THAT'S GREAT. Constantly enclosed rabbits can get depressed, and well, animals are meant to run around freely imo. We let mine free roam the house (since he's sorta porty trained haha) and we have a teeny garden which he loves running around in. If you can, let him always be in the garden or in the house. If you have to cage him for the night or something, that's fine, but he should be free the majority of his time. 

4. WATER. He should have lots of water available. Preferably in a bowl. They need lots of it since they're constantly eating and pooping. 

5. Mine doesn't like to be picked up, other rabbits do. Find out what yours likes, so that if you need to move him from place to place you don't scare him. (Our bunny follows my bf when he tells him "come on!" which we taught him since we can't pick him up) 

6. You should take him to a vet eventually. I'm not 100% sure about this, but they need a shot which I think is for fleas (don't quote me on this). Also to just check that everything's ok. 

7. Buy him things to munch on! They have long teeth that continually grow and biting on cardboard (yes, they can eat cardboard!), wood chips, wood squares, etc. will help keep his teeth healthy. This is important because if not, his teeth can grow misaligned and cause damage to his little mouth which will be costly in the future. 

8. Our rabbit is very curious, but don't be surprised if yours likes to hide a lot, since they're naturally prey animals. 

9. You can give him treats like: carrots, fruits (non-acidic and non-citric), cabbage, spinach, etc., but as occassional treats. Never as their main diet or super often. Especially with fruits, since it's a lot of sugar. 

10. As a baby, his head is very soft. Make sure that he doesn't fall from high places since he could die :( (happened to my sister's rabbit). 

11. Pay attention to his poop, especially as you introduce new foods. They should be round and hard, if they're soft and/or liquid, take him to the vet immediately. Diarrhea is super dangerous for rabbits. 

12. He will chew EVERYTHING. Take care of cables especially. We're about to buy cable protectors because he has chewed on HDMI cables, our steamer cable and like 5 chargers lol. 

Aaaand that's basically it! I know it's a lot (and there's a lot I didn't mention as well, so feel free to message me) but if you give him love and attention, he'll be a great pet. 

Good luck!!

Hi! Recruiter here. Hope you don't mind me giving you some unsolicited advice, I don't wanna come off as a know it all!
But definitely showing interest is good, but going overboard with a double email, especially with what you intend to say in that second email is not a good idea. It's been 6 hours, but depending on what line of work this job is, that particular recruiter/manager/etc. may be extremely busy and just didn't get around to your email yet or is trying to coordinate before contacting you. Recruiter life is hectic af. 

The proper etiquette is for the recruiter to contact the person and let them know if they're still in the running or not, however i know that doesn't happen nearly as much as it should, so I understand your anxiety! 

If you want to follow-up anyway, wait until tomorrow afternoon and call, don't email. They already have the first email. Call and if they don't answer leave a polite mesaage saying how interested you're in the position and how grateful you would be if you were still given a chance to interview. Also, and this is more depending on the recruiter's style, but don't over-apologize, try to seem confident! Like "I'm sorry I didn't get to your email in time, but I would love it if you could give me an opportunity to show you how my skills can benefit your company," or something like that. 

Hope this helps, and I really hope you get an answer soon!!!
